title: Enemies
hookLine: bring back your enemy's ox: love, do good, bless and pray, from the Torah to Jesus to Paul

cards: Tucked among the laws in Exodus is one that sounds oddly specific: "If thou meet thine enemy's ox or his ass going astray, thou shalt surely bring it back to him again." Not your friend's ox. Your enemy's.
The one person whose lost donkey you might quietly enjoy hearing about. And the next verse goes further: if his donkey has collapsed under its load, help him lift it.

In the Torah, the law is already asking for this: a small, practical good, done for someone you can't stand. This path first heard love your enemies on day two hundred forty-seven; today, how practical it gets.

teach.b: Jesus takes that thread and pulls it tight. In Luke's Gospel he says: "Love your enemies, do good to them which hate you, Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you."
The verbs are practical: love, do good, bless, pray. Most of them are things you do with your hands or your mouth. None of them asks you to pretend the person is your friend.
Paul writes it to Rome, as short as he can make it: "Bless them which persecute you: bless, and curse not."
The Greek word for bless there means, at its simplest, to speak well of. So the command is about your words. When the person comes up, in conversation or in your own head, you don't curse them.
You speak well, or you wish them well.

teach.h: IF THINE ENEMY HUNGER, FEED HIM.
teach.b: Then Paul quotes Proverbs: "if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head." Readers differ about the coals.
Some hear the burn of shame that might turn an enemy around. Others hear something gentler. The first half isn't in doubt: feed him.
None of this undoes what came two days ago.

Doing good to an enemy isn't the same as walking back into harm. You can send the ox home without moving in with its owner. What these texts ask is narrower and harder: no curses, and one concrete good.

how: Christians pray for their enemies by name in private prayer and in church intercessions, and try to answer hostility with practical kindness, citing Luke 6:27–28 and Romans 12:14–21.

o: rivals you may quietly curse if you stay polite
foreign armies Israel was told to drive away
those who hate you, whom Jesus says to love and bless

p: if thine enemy hunger, feed him

s: the Exodus law asks you to return only a friend's stray ox
Exodus 23:4 says "thine enemy's ox": bring it back to him again.
Paul's coals-of-fire line is a quotation from Proverbs
Romans 12:20 quotes Proverbs 25:21–22: feed your hungry enemy.
Jesus asks only that you stop hating your enemies
he names four actions: love, do good, bless, and pray for them.

games.q: you're walking home and see your enemy's donkey wandering loose on the road. he'd never do the same for you. what does Exodus say?
o: leave it; it's not your problem.
tell the neighbors whose donkey is loose.
games.why: "thou shalt surely bring it back to him again." the law asks for a small, practical good done for someone you can't stand.

practice: Bring to mind someone you find hard, a rival, a critic, someone who has wronged you, and notice what your mind says about them first, without scolding yourself for it.
Then try Paul's turn: wish them one specific good thing, a good night's sleep, a worry that lifts, and hold that wish for a few breaths, even if it feels thin.
If you pray, you can do what Jesus asks in Luke and pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Enemies. The people Jesus tells his followers to love, do good to, bless and pray for, starting with one practical good.

orig.note: Greek: bless, speak well of; the command in Luke 6:28 and Romans 12:14.

carryVoice: Your line: bless, do not curse. To bless is to speak well of. Rest well.
